# Spherical Harmonics Optimization
Also called: SH Optimization, SH Compression, SH Distillation

## Overview
This family encompasses methods that optimize the Spherical Harmonics (SH) representation within 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to reduce memory footprint, accelerate rendering, or improve training stability. While standard 3DGS uses third-order SH (16 coefficients per channel) to model view-dependent color, these techniques either compress the coefficients via quantization [14181-spherical-harmonics-vector-quantization.md], distill them into lower degrees [9467-first-order-spherical-harmonics-distillation.md], or eliminate unnecessary computations [S1, unofficial]. They differ from [Explicit Camera Jacobian Derivation](10077-explicit-camera-jacobian-derivation.md) by focusing on the radiance representation rather than gradient efficiency, and from [Efficient Multi-View Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting](13982-efficient-multi-view-training-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md) by targeting the SH data structure specifically.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family operate on the SH coefficients $\mathbf{c}_i$ associated with each 3D Gaussian primitive. In standard 3DGS, these coefficients are stored as floating-point values (typically FP32 or FP16) and represent the radiance function $L(\omega)$ as a linear combination of SH basis functions. The optimization strategies share the goal of reducing the computational or memory cost of evaluating or storing these coefficients without significantly degrading the rendered image quality.

## Subtopics

### [First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation](9467-first-order-spherical-harmonics-distillation.md)
Reduces the view-dependent color representation from third-order to first-order SH to decrease parameter count and rendering computation [9467-first-order-spherical-harmonics-distillation.md]. It uses knowledge distillation where a "student" model with first-order SH approximates a pretrained "teacher" model with third-order SH, preserving visual fidelity better than simple truncation [9467-first-order-spherical-harmonics-distillation.md]. Choose this when memory bandwidth is the bottleneck and high-frequency view-dependent effects are not critical. See [First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation](9467-first-order-spherical-harmonics-distillation.md).

### [Explicit Camera Jacobian Derivation](10077-explicit-camera-jacobian-derivation.md)
Derives analytical Jacobians of the SE(3) camera pose with respect to 3DGS primitives to enable efficient, differentiable camera tracking without automatic differentiation overhead [10077-explicit-camera-jacobian-derivation.md]. It solves the computational expense of gradient computation in SLAM systems by providing minimal parameterization on the Lie group [10077-explicit-camera-jacobian-derivation.md]. Choose this for real-time SLAM applications where tracking speed is paramount. See [Explicit Camera Jacobian Derivation](10077-explicit-camera-jacobian-derivation.md).

### [Efficient Multi-View Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting](13982-efficient-multi-view-training-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md)
Enables stable optimization by training on multiple views per iteration, reducing mini-batch gradient variance compared to single-view approaches [13982-efficient-multi-view-training-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. It uses thread-efficient partial rendering to overcome tile-based rasterizer overhead and introduces a 3D-space compatible densification mechanism for Adaptive Density Control (ADC) [13982-efficient-multi-view-training-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. Choose this when training on large multi-view datasets to improve convergence stability. See [Efficient Multi-View Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting](13982-efficient-multi-view-training-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md).

### [Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization](14181-spherical-harmonics-vector-quantization.md)
Compresses 3DGS by replacing per-splat SH coefficients with indices pointing to a shared palette of distinct SH vectors, reducing memory footprint at the cost of minor lighting artifacts [14181-spherical-harmonics-vector-quantization.md]. It retains higher-order SH information through clustering rather than reducing the degree, differing from distillation methods [14181-spherical-harmonics-vector-quantization.md]. Choose this when storage size is the primary constraint. See [Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization](14181-spherical-harmonics-vector-quantization.md).

### SH Degree Zero Optimization
Sets the maximum degree of Spherical Harmonics coefficients to 0 to remove superfluous operations and improve training speed [S1, unofficial]. It modifies the model code to delete operations relative to the max degree, as features represented by SH coefficients with degree > 0 remain unchanged during training in the original 3DGS implementation [S1, unofficial]. This yields a 16.25% improvement in training speed by default, and up to 16.57% with specific code changes, with no explicit impact on final rendering quality [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The use of Spherical Harmonics in 3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced in the original 3DGS paper [12] (cited in [S1, unofficial]), which utilized third-order SH to capture view-dependent appearance. Subsequent research identified inefficiencies in this representation. [S1, unofficial] observed that in the standard implementation, higher-degree SH coefficients often remain static during training, suggesting they are superfluous for many scenes. This led to optimizations like setting the degree to zero [S1, unofficial]. Other works focused on compressing the high-dimensional SH vectors (45 coefficients per splat excluding base color) using vector quantization [14181-spherical-harmonics-vector-quantization.md] or distilling them into lower degrees [9467-first-order-spherical-harmonics-distillation.md]. These methods address the growing memory demands of large-scale 3DGS scenes.

## Sources
